passage:
Anand's team meeting at the design studio always ended the same way. “You're all professionals, work it out,” Anand said, closing the laptop. In the first month it felt like a gift; nobody hovered. Madhuri picked her own projects and enjoyed it. By the third month two people were building the same feature, a client call had no owner, and nobody knew which deadline was real.

In the corridor Ritesh muttered, “Who's deciding?” Lakshmi said nothing and looked at the floor. Madhuri found herself refreshing Anand's calendar, hoping for a slot to ask what mattered most this quarter. The next free slot was in three weeks. She closed the tab, and her jaw tightened.

qa.q: What did Anand say at the end of team meetings?
qa.a: Anand said, “You're all professionals, work it out.”

qa.q: Why did Madhuri's jaw tighten at the end?
qa.a: Madhuri felt frustrated and unsupported, needing direction and finding nobody available to give it.

qa.q: What choice could Madhuri make instead of waiting three weeks?
qa.a: Madhuri could write down the questions and proposed priorities, share them with the team and ask Anand to confirm by message.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi, who looked at the floor, be feeling?
qa.a: Lakshmi may be equally confused and frustrated but afraid that saying so would sound like complaining.

grounding: A team with a leader who sets no direction feels confused and unsupported as freedom turns into drift and quiet frustration.

passage:
Dear Deepak,

I'm writing rather than catching you in the corridor because I want to say this calmly. When you took over the team in April, the freedom felt great. I chose my own tasks and finished early. But lately two of us built overlapping features, a client asked me something I couldn't answer, and Kavita is redoing work I had already done. Meera says she has stopped asking questions in meetings because “nothing changes.” I'm not angry with you; I just feel adrift.

Could we agree on the top three priorities for the quarter and who owns what? I'm happy to draft it.

Thanks,
Uma

qa.q: What did the freedom feel like when Deepak took over in April?
qa.a: The freedom felt great, and Uma chose tasks and finished early.

qa.q: What does Uma mean by saying, “I just feel adrift”?
qa.a: Uma feels directionless and unsupported, unsure what matters most, though not angry.

qa.q: What did Uma ask Deepak to agree on?
qa.a: Uma asked Deepak to agree on the top three priorities for the quarter and who owns what.

qa.q: How might Meera feel, having stopped asking questions because “nothing changes”?
qa.a: Meera probably feels discouraged and resigned, believing that speaking up will not bring direction.

grounding: A team member writes to a hands-off leader that freedom has turned into drift, confusion and quiet frustration, and asks for priorities.

passage:
I'm Sabina, and my first manager, Rehana, was the nicest person I've ever worked for. That was part of the problem.
On day one she said, “Do whatever you think is best. I trust you.” I loved it. For two weeks, I felt so free. I set my own hours and picked my own tasks.
Then I realised I didn't know what the team was actually aiming for. Three of us made three different versions of the same report. When I asked Rehana which one she wanted, she smiled and said, “Whatever you think.”
By the third month, I was frustrated all the time and I didn't even know at whom. Nobody was doing anything wrong. There just wasn't any direction.

qa.q: What did Rehana say on day one?
qa.a: She said, "Do whatever you think is best. I trust you."

qa.q: How did Sabina's feelings change over the first three months?
qa.a: Sabina felt free and happy at first, then confused, and by the third month frustrated all the time.

qa.q: What could Sabina ask Rehana for?
qa.a: Sabina could ask for two or three clear goals for the quarter and a short weekly check-in, so freedom has a direction.

qa.q: How might the other two colleagues who made reports have felt?
qa.a: They were probably frustrated too, having done duplicate work without knowing what was needed.

grounding: A young employee recalls a hands-off manager whose freedom felt good at first, then turned into drift, confusion and quiet frustration.

passage:
Mentor's note on Indu, new analyst, quarterly check-in.
Indu joined Leela's team four months ago. Leela is known to be relaxed; she rarely sets deadlines or gives feedback. In our first talk, Indu was delighted: “I can work how I like!”
Today she was different. She said she'd spent two weeks on a market study, only to learn in a meeting that the client had changed direction a month ago and nobody told her. “I don't even know if I'm doing well or badly,” she said, twisting her pen.
I suggested she ask Leela for a short weekly meeting and write down three goals together. I will also speak to Leela, gently, about setting direction for new staff.

qa.q: How long did Indu spend on the market study?
qa.a: She spent two weeks on it.

qa.q: How did Indu feel at this check-in?
qa.a: She felt confused and frustrated, twisting her pen and unsure whether she was doing well or badly.

qa.q: Why is a weekly meeting and three goals a helpful step?
qa.a: It adds the direction Leela hasn't set, so Indu knows what matters and gets regular feedback.

qa.q: How might Leela see her relaxed style?
qa.a: She probably sees it as trusting and kind, not realising it leaves new staff drifting.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a young analyst under a hands-off manager, where early freedom turns into confusion and frustration.

passage:
Thursday
Another week, another meeting where Nandini asked, “So, what's everyone working on?” and then nodded at everything.
When I joined, I thought having no rules was the best thing ever. I made my own plan. Now it's month five and I have no idea if my plan matters. Three projects are half-finished. Nobody decides which one is important.
Today Arjun and I found out we'd both been building the same dashboard. Two weeks each. Wasted.
I'm angry, but at what? Nandini is kind. She just never says where we're going. It's like being on a bus with no driver.
Tomorrow I'll ask her to pick one priority for the team. Just one.
Samir

qa.q: What had Arjun and Samir both been building?
qa.a: The same dashboard.

qa.q: How is Samir feeling in month five?
qa.a: Samir feels angry and confused, frustrated at wasted work and no clear direction.

qa.q: Is asking Nandini for one priority a good step, and why?
qa.a: Yes; one clear priority gives the team direction and stops duplicate work, without attacking Nandini.

qa.q: How might Arjun feel about the wasted two weeks?
qa.a: Arjun likely feels frustrated too, having spent effort on work that didn't need doing twice.

grounding: A young employee writes about a hands-off manager, where the early freedom has turned into drift, confusion and anger.

passage:

Gopika: third week of "you guys figure it out" 😐

Shalini: want to ask him for 15 mins together? just 3 questions: goal, deadline, who owns what
Gopika: yes. writing it now
Gopika: and sending it to Vikram too so we stop duplicating

qa.q: Who else is making a version of the deck?
qa.a: Vikram is doing a version too.

qa.q: How is Gopika feeling by the third week?
qa.a: Gopika feels tired and frustrated, redoing slides three ways without knowing what Rakesh wants, while still caring about the client.

qa.q: What do Gopika and Shalini decide to ask for, and why could it help?
qa.a: Fifteen minutes with Rakesh and three questions, goal, deadline and who owns what, which gives the team the direction it lacks.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel about Rakesh's style at first?
qa.a: Shalini loved the freedom in the first week, with no micromanaging, before it turned into confusion.

grounding: Shows a team under a leader who sets no direction, enjoying the freedom at first and then drifting into confusion and quiet frustration.
